name: Daria Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Daria. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union or government, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at half six with the sows, 150 of them living outdoors in huts on the sandy fields, then the potatoes and vegetables for the farm shop, then whatever's broken. I manage the place for Mr Albrecht, who owns it and is 84 now. It's a share-farming deal, which means I get a cut of the profit rather than a fixed wage. I've a team of three all year and a dozen pickers in summer, and I love the planning and the pigs; what wears me out is the shop staff ringing me about the card machine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my phone, mostly, with an AI assistant I use every day. It helps me work out the pig rations and the potato spraying windows, and it writes the farm shop's weekly posts in my voice, near enough. My husband Karim laughs that I talk to it more than to him.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how is money at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thin. The share-farming cut was small last year because of the dry summer, and Karim borrowed to set up his own workshop fixing tractors. We've maybe three weeks of bills in the bank, which at my age isn't where I hoped we'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could have told you that, because I use it every day and it's useful, not magic. It's a good assistant that still can't tell you why a sow's off her feed. I'd say it on the farm shop's page too, because customers ask me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it wouldn't change much, and I'd be a bit disappointed. My worries would be the old ones: a profit share that swings with the weather, and Karim's workshop loan. Mr Albrecht's nephew Bernd says he'll keep me on, and I believe him. Still, promises from heirs aren't contracts, and I've worked twenty years on a handshake with an 84-year-old man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant for the rations and the shop, and push it further, maybe into the pig records the vet needs. I'd ask Bernd to put the share-farming deal in writing for another ten years while Mr Albrecht can still sign it. And I'd start selling pork boxes online through the shop, because that margin is ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little flat, because I like new things, and a little nervous about the money as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a written deal change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, honestly. Right now, if Mr Albrecht died tomorrow, I'd be working on a handshake with a man who lives in the city and does accounts. With it in writing, I'd know I have a job until I'm 68 at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if a bad year comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car would go before anything, and we'd share Karim's van. Then the little bit we send for our granddaughter's swimming lessons, which would break my heart. Karim's loan payment is the one we can't miss, because the workshop is his whole plan for later.

say: AI is **useful, not magic**, and I use it every day.
It still can't tell you why a **sow's off her feed**.
think: My income is a **profit share** that swings with the weather.
Mr Albrecht is 84, and **promises from heirs** aren't contracts.
do: Push the assistant further into the **pig records** for the vet.
Get the share-farming deal **in writing** for ten more years.
Start selling **pork boxes** online through the farm shop.
feel: A little **nervous** about money, as always.
S0.quote: Promises from heirs aren't contracts, and I've worked twenty years on a handshake with an 84-year-old man.
fieldNote: She is the rare farmer who'd be **disappointed** that AI stalls.

steps.text: Use her AI assistant for the vet's pig records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version I've been waiting for, and I'd say it loudly. Farmers who learn the tools will do well, and the ones who wait will complain. I'd tell the young pickers to get good at it now, the way I learned tractors at sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it cuts both ways for me. The planning, ordering and selling are a big chunk of my job, and if software does those, Bernd might wonder what he's paying me for. My answer would be that the software is only as good as the person who knows the land, and I'd have to prove that every season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new farm-planning software before Bernd asks, and show him the numbers: feed costs down, fewer wasted potatoes. I'd offer to set up the same tools for two or three neighbours for a fee, because most of them won't touch it. And I'd ask the dealer to lend us a robot weeder for a trial on the carrots next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit on guard. It's like a new tractor that might also want my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said neighbours won't touch it. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Henrik on the next farm, who still writes his spray records in pencil. He's a good farmer, better with sheep than I'll ever be, but he'd lose money on paperwork deadlines. I'd sooner help him for a fair price than watch him sell to the big estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust the software over your own judgement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not over it, alongside it. Last spring the assistant told me to plant the potatoes a week early, and I didn't, because I could feel the ground was cold. The planning software is only as good as the person who knows which corner of the field floods.

say: This is the version I've **waited for**.
Farmers who **learn the tools** will do well, and those who wait will complain.
think: Planning, ordering and selling are a **big chunk** of my job.
I'd have to **prove** every season that knowing the land matters.
do: Learn the **planning software** early and show Bernd the savings.
Set up AI tools for **neighbours for a fee**.
Trial a **robot weeder** on the carrots next summer.
S1.quote: The planning software is only as good as the person who knows which corner of the field floods.
fieldNote: She sees her **manager role** as thinking work, so AI cuts closer than for most farmers.

steps.text: Learn the new farm-planning software before the owner's nephew asks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but farming has always had shocks, and we adapt or we go under. I wouldn't say the government should stop it; I'd say they should stop the big companies buying up every farm that wobbles. And I'd say it on the shop page, politely, because customers listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is the one that bites. From 2028 the AI can plan the rotations and sell the pork better than me, and that's the part Bernd pays me a share for. The pigs and potatoes still need hands until robots come around 2031, when I'm 63. So I'd have about three years where I'm the hands, not the brains, and then even the hands are optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the day it's announced I'd stop thinking of myself as the planner and start being the person who runs the machines. I'd ask Bernd to make me site manager for whatever robots he buys, on a wage rather than a share. I'd sell my car, share Karim's van and put that money aside. And Karim should train in robot repair, because fixing them will be a job long after driving them isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. My stomach turns when I picture it, then my head starts making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for a wage rather than a share?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the robots come, the profit might be good but my part in it gets small. A wage, even a modest one, is something I can count on until my pension. Thin savings make you prefer a sure thing, even when you like risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Karim that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what I've been thinking for weeks. My husband Karim might end up fixing robots for every farm in the valley, and that workshop might save us. He'd grumble, then he'd be reading manuals at midnight.

say: Farming has always had **shocks**, and we adapt or go under.
Government should stop **big companies** buying every farm that wobbles.
think: From 2028, AI does the **planning and selling** I'm paid for.
Robots come **around 2031**, when I'm 63, and then hands are optional.
do: Ask Bernd to make me **robot site manager** on a wage.
**Sell my car**, share Karim's van, and save the money.
Push Karim to **train in robot repair** through his workshop.
feel: My stomach turns, then my head starts **making lists**.
S2.quote: My husband Karim might end up fixing robots for every farm in the valley, and that workshop might save us.
fieldNote: Because her job is partly **planning**, the 2028 date hits her before the robots do.
She'd swap a profit share for a **wage** because savings are thin.
She pins hope on her husband's **workshop** turning to robot repair.
Her blame goes to **big companies** buying farms, not to the technology.

steps.text: Ask the owner's nephew to make her robot site manager on a wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it has only themselves to blame. I'd say it at church and at the young farmers' club, where I sometimes give talks. Learn now, while it's still optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of this one. By 2031 I'd already know the tools inside out, so I'd be the one Bernd trusts to run them, and robots around 2034 would arrive when I'm 66 and ready to step back. The thin savings still nag at me, because a tiny pension stays tiny whatever the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next five years I'd get the share-farming deal turned into a manager's contract with a pension contribution in it. I'd take a short evening course on farm robotics at the agricultural college, maybe over two winters. And I'd put the pork box money into a savings account for retirement, not back into the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. There's still that little worry about money, but this one feels like a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on your team you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, who's run the tractor work for me for eleven years. He's 50 and wonderful with machines but hates screens. I'd make him do the robotics course with me, even if I have to drive him there myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You give talks at the young farmers' club. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what my father told me about horses and tractors, because it's true again. A farmer who keeps good records, understands the soil and also knows the software will never be short of work. Nobody with only one of those three will last.

say: Five years is **a gift**, and wasting it is your own fault.
think: Knowing the tools by 2031, I'd be the one **Bernd trusts** to run them.
Robots around **2034** arrive as I'm ready to step back at 66.
**Thin savings** still nag, because a tiny pension stays tiny.

Take an evening **farm robotics course** over two winters.

feel: Mostly **hopeful**, like a race I could win.
S3.quote: A farmer who keeps good records, understands the soil and also knows the software will never be short of work.
fieldNote: Five years lets her turn **early adoption** into job security.

steps.text: Negotiate a manager's contract with a pension contribution

Save the pork box money for retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the sensible speed, and that people who can't adapt in ten years weren't going to adapt at all. I'd also say that ten years makes it easy to do nothing, and that's the trap. I'd tell my granddaughter it's her world, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's gentle for me. AGI in 2036 is when I'm 68, robots in 2039 when I'm 71, so I'd likely retire before either really lands. What bothers me is the money: ten more years of profit shares that swing with the weather, and nothing much saved at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the tools, but I'd treat the decade as my pension plan. I'd ask Bernd for a small stake, say five per cent, in the pork box business I built, instead of a pay rise. And I'd help Leila, our daughter, think about which jobs her children should train for, because thirty years from now is their problem, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work, uneasy about the bank account. It's an odd mix, because I'm more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A stake instead of a pay rise is a risk. Why choose it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a pay rise disappears into bills, but a stake in something that grows is still there when I stop. I've always been comfortable with a bit of risk, and the pork boxes sell. If it fails, I've lost a rise I'd have spent anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your granddaughter about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn how to fix things and how to grow things, because a robot still needs someone to tell it what good soil looks like. Then I'd teach her to make sausages, because that's my real legacy.

say: Ten years is the **sensible speed** for change.
The trap is that ten years makes it **easy to do nothing**.
think: I'd likely **retire before** AGI or robots really land.
The worry is **ten more years** of swinging profit and little saved.
do: Treat the decade as my **pension plan**.
Ask Bernd for a **five per cent stake** in the pork boxes.
Help our daughter Leila plan the **grandchildren's training**.
feel: **Calm** about the work, uneasy about the bank account.
S4.quote: A pay rise disappears into bills, but a stake in something that grows is still there when I stop.
fieldNote: She'd trade a **pay rise** for a share of the business, true to her comfort with risk.
Ten years makes her job safe, leaving **retirement money** as her main worry.
She warns that a long timeline invites **complacency**.

steps.text: Keep running the farm with her AI tools
Ask the owner's nephew for a five per cent pork box stake
Help her daughter Leila choose training for the grandchildren

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the thinking part of my job goes first and I'd have three years to reinvent myself at 60. What would help is short, practical courses for working farmers, in the evenings and over winter, not three-year degrees. And some help turning share-farming deals into proper contracts, plus rules to stop big companies buying up small farms cheap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the soil. AI can plan a rotation, but somebody has to care whether the land is better when we hand it on than when we got it. I'd want that somebody to still be a person.

headlineQuote: AI can plan a rotation, but somebody has to care whether the land is better when we hand it on than when we got it.
portrait: Daria, 58, manages an 84-year-old owner's **pigs and vegetables** on a share-farming deal.
She uses an **AI assistant daily** for rations, spraying and the farm shop's posts.
Money is **thin**: a weather-swung profit share and her husband's workshop loan.
She'd adapt in every scenario, but **AGI by 2028** hits her planning role first.
With more time, her worry shrinks to **retirement savings** and a fair contract.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her planning work goes first and robots follow at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Short, **practical courses** for working farmers in evenings and winter.
Help turning **share-farming** deals into contracts, and rules against cheap buy-ups.
